in this way not only is it possible to reach the ever-varying times of the best market prices in Europe, but it is also possible to reconcile a cultivation of serious proportions with early production, avoiding as much as possible the disease that sometimes affects certain localities in the months of February and March. And we will add by the way, that even in this unfortunate case the field should not be abandoned as a lost cause, especially if the tomato begins to fruit, for with some attentions, such as watering, cleaning, etc., what is believed to be a complete ruin still yields greater profits than if the land were dedicated to an ordinary crop.

TRANSPLANTING:

After several setbacks and no few trials, we believe we can affirm that the planting ground must be thoroughly loosened with deep plowing or harrowing, and that its fertility should not be excessive so as not to favor the development of foliage to the detriment of fruiting.

PALISADE.
After the last weeding, the
palisade must be formed in which the tomato plant is gradually accommodated during its development.
We begin by making with
a bar blow holes about 025
centimeters deep along each
furrow and about 1'30 apart,
ensuring they face each other in each pair of furrows. Into these holes we insert stakes that emerge from the ground
about 1 1/2 meters, then inclining each pole towards its companion in the corresponding
furrow to tie them at their free ends, at which point a horizontal rod is also secured that runs along the top of the palisade. To complete the framework, we then fix several horizontal rods or poles arranged
horizontally and at different heights.
This system of inclined-plane palisade we consider advantageous over the vertical palisade:
1.° For offering greater resistance to
strong winds or storms.
2.° Because in large-scale plantings there is not always
personnel to
attend to the tomato patch in time, allowing the foliage to take over the walkways.
3.°
Because in winter cultivation
the invigorating action of the sun's rays is directly on a larger surface of the
plant.
4.° Because it is probable that with
less verticality of the branches, fruiting is favored, with slower
circulation of the descending sap.

this delicate cultivation is the pruning and clearing of the plant, as well as the removal

of secondary branches up to a height of

and leaves, so that the fruits and inner parts of the plants are well ventilated.

No puede establecerse un número fijo
por depender principalmente de las con-

GUANO.
Algunos agricultores colocan al pié de
las plantas, de ordinario entre el segun-
do y tercer brote ele la florescencia, un
poco de guano; y si bien aun no hemos
podido formarnos un juicio definitivo,
nos parece que este abono modifica en
sentido desfavorable las condiciones aro-
máticas y sabor agradable del tomate, sin
contar con que entra más pronto en des-
composición.
RECOLECCIÓN.
El tomate debe cogerse así que empie-
za á colorear por su vértice ó parte
opuesta al pedúnculo ó ramilla queje su-
jeta á la planta, procurando que esta
operación se efectúe con el mayor esme-
ro y con tiempo claro, entre 8 de la ma-
ñana y 4 de la tarde. Por ningún concep-
to debe hacerse la recolección estando
el tomate húmedo ó mojado—y este con-
sejo lo hacemos estensivo á toda clase de
frutos—sino cuando se halle seco y bien
soleado, para que dure su máximo de tiem-
po sin entraren putrefacción.

WATERING.
A fixed number cannot be established
as it depends mainly on the conditions of the soil and external agents, although speaking in general terms it can be affirmed that the tomato plant is
not very demanding. Furthermore, we all know that watering must be frequent when the fruit is forming and during periods
of continuous heat.
GUANO.
Some farmers place at the base of
the plants, usually between the second and third shoot of the flowering, a
little guano; and although we have not yet
been able to form a definitive judgment,
it seems to us that this fertilizer modifies in
an unfavorable sense the aromatic conditions and pleasant flavor of the tomato, not
to mention that it decomposes more quickly.
HARVEST.
The tomato should be picked as soon as it begins to color at its apex or the part
opposite to the peduncle or small branch that attaches it to the plant, ensuring that this
operation is carried out with the utmost care and in clear weather, between 8 in the morning and 4 in the afternoon. Under no circumstances should the harvest be done when
the tomato is wet or damp—and this advice we extend to all kinds
of fruits—unless it is dry and well
sun-dried, so that it lasts its maximum time without entering into putrefaction.
